turns.prompt_text: I would like to create a google cloud automation script to sort, organize, and move google photos from google photos into my google drive
turns.response_html:
This is a complex task because Google Photos and Google Drive have been completely separated (as of 2019). There is no longer a native "sync" feature, and the Google Photos API has strict limitations to prevent accidental data loss.

Because you are looking for an automation solution, I have gathered perspectives from cloud architects, data archivists, and lightweight scripters. Here are the three distinct ways to approach this, ranging from "low code" to "enterprise-grade" automation.

Critical Constraints (The "Archivist" Perspective)

Before writing any code, it is vital to understand the limitations imposed by Google to protect user data:

  1. Copy, Don't Move: The Google Photos API does not allow third-party apps (including your script) to delete photos. You can only copy them to Drive. You will have to manually delete them from Photos afterward to free up space.
  2. Metadata Stripping: When you download a photo via the API, Google often strips GPS data for privacy unless you explicitly handle the scope correctly.
  3. Compression: The API generally serves the "High Quality" version, not necessarily the original file bit-for-bit, unless you grab the specific baseUrl with download parameters.

Option 1: The "Lightweight" Approach (Google Apps Script)

Best for: Users who want a free, serverless solution without setting up a billing account.

This runs directly inside Google’s ecosystem. It requires JavaScript knowledge but handles authentication much easier than Python.

  1. Go to script.google.com.
  2. Enable the Drive API and Photos Library API in the "Services" tab.
  3. Use the following logic to create a time-based trigger (automation):
function copyPhotosToDrive() {
  // 1. Search for photos (e.g., from a specific date range)
  var searchUrl = "https://photoslibrary.googleapis.com/v1/mediaItems:search";
  // Note: Requires complex OAuth2 setup in Apps Script manifest to access Photos API directly
  
  // 2. Fetch the image blob
  var imageBlob = UrlFetchApp.fetch(photoUrl).getBlob();
  
  // 3. Create folder in Drive based on metadata
  var folder = DriveApp.createFolder("2024-Backup");
  
  // 4. Save file
  folder.createFile(imageBlob);
}

Note: Apps Script has a 6-minute execution limit. If you have thousands of photos, this script will time out. You must write logic to use "continuation tokens" to resume the job in batches.

Option 2: The "Engineer" Approach (Python on Google Cloud)

Best for: Robust, scheduled automation that handles thousands of files.

This approach uses a Google Cloud Function (serverless) or a local Python script. This allows for better error handling and file organization.

Prerequisites

  1. Create a Project in the .
  2. Enable Google Photos Library API and Google Drive API.
  3. Create OAuth 2.0 Credentials (Download the credentials.json file).

The Automation Logic (Python)

You will need the google-auth, google-auth-oauthlib, and requests libraries.

1. Authentication: You must perform an OAuth handshake. The scope required is https://www.googleapis.com/auth/photoslibrary.readonly.

2. The Sorting & Organization Script: This script fetches media, checks the date, creates a hierarchy in Drive (Year > Month), and uploads.

import requests
from googleapiclient.discovery import build

def organize_and_move(creds):
    # Setup Clients
    photos_service = build('photoslibrary', 'v1', credentials=creds, static_discovery=False)
    drive_service = build('drive', 'v3', credentials=creds)

    # 1. List Media Items (Pagination is key here)
    results = photos_service.mediaItems().list(pageSize=100).execute()
    items = results.get('mediaItems', [])

    for item in items:
        filename = item['filename']
        # Metadata is inside 'mediaMetadata' -> 'creationTime'
        creation_time = item['mediaMetadata']['creationTime'] 
        year = creation_time[:4]
        month = creation_time[5:7]

        # 2. Check/Create Drive Folder Hierarchy (Year/Month)
        # (Requires a helper function to check if folder exists in Drive)
        folder_id = get_or_create_drive_folder(drive_service, year, month)

        # 3. Download the Photo
        # Append '=d' to download the original quality
        download_url = item['baseUrl'] + "=d"
        response = requests.get(download_url)

        # 4. Upload to Drive
        if response.status_code == 200:
            file_metadata = {'name': filename, 'parents': [folder_id]}
            # Use MediaIoBaseUpload for uploading bytes
            # ... (upload logic) ...
            print(f"Moved {filename} to Drive/{year}/{month}")

Option 3: The "Data Sovereign" Approach (Rclone)

Best for: People who prefer open-source tools over writing their own code.

If you don't want to maintain a script, the command-line tool Rclone is the industry standard for this. It is a pre-built automation tool that "speaks" both Drive and Photos APIs.

  1. Install Rclone.
  2. Run rclone config and authorize both Google Photos and Google Drive.
  3. Run a single command to sync and organize: 
    rclone copy "gphotos:media/by-year" "gdrive:PhotosBackup" --progress
  • Perspective: Many system administrators prefer this because Rclone handles the retry logic, API limits, and throttling automatically, which are very difficult to code from scratch in Python.

turns.prompt_text: Maybe this isn't a good idea, I just need better categorization and sorting in Google Photos, some automated script to go through and be a digital butler is nice
turns.response_html:
This is a wise pivot. As you suspected, the "Move to Drive" plan is often a trap because Google intentionally broke the link between Photos and Drive in 2019. Moving files often strips them of their "cloud intelligence" (face grouping, location data) and turns them into dumb files.

To achieve your "Digital Butler" goal within Google Photos, you have to work around the "Read-Heavy, Write-Light" nature of the Google Photos API.

The "Butler" Constraints

To write this script, you must understand the rules the "Butler" must follow, which I've synthesized from the developer documentation and data-archivist communities:

The Butler CAN DoThe Butler CANNOT Do
Create Albums (e.g., "Receipts 2025")Delete Photos (API prohibits this safety risk)
Read "Content Categories" (e.g., identifying Cats, Documents, Selfies)Archive Photos (API cannot "hide" photos from the main feed)
Filter by Date/CameraModify User-Created Albums (It can only manage albums it created)

The Solution: "The Albumizer" Script

Since we cannot "move" files out of the main feed (Archive) via code, the best automation strategy is Smart Album Tagging.

We will write a Python script that acts as a "Butler" by asking Google: "Show me all the Receipts from 2025," and then forcibly grouping them into a tidy Album. This doesn't clean the main feed, but it gives you organized buckets instantly.

1. Setup (The Annoying Part)

You still need a Google Cloud Project with the Photos Library API enabled.

  1. Go to Google Cloud Console.
  2. Create a project -> Enable Photos Library API.
  3. OAuth Consent Screen: Set to "External" (since it's for you) and add your email as a "Test User."
  4. Credentials: Create "OAuth Client ID" (Desktop App) -> Download credentials.json.

2. The Code (Python)

This script requires pip install google-auth-oauthlib google-auth-httplib2 google-api-python-client.

It defines a "Butler" function that takes a Category (defined by Google) and a Date Range, finds the photos, and puts them in an Album.

import os
import pickle
from google_auth_oauthlib.flow import InstalledAppFlow
from google.auth.transport.requests import Request
from googleapiclient.discovery import build

# Setup Permissions
SCOPES = ['https://www.googleapis.com/auth/photoslibrary']

def get_service():
    creds = None
    if os.path.exists('token.pickle'):
        with open('token.pickle', 'rb') as token:
            creds = pickle.load(token)
    if not creds or not creds.valid:
        if creds and creds.expired and creds.refresh_token:
            creds.refresh(Request())
        else:
            flow = InstalledAppFlow.from_client_secrets_file(
                'credentials.json', SCOPES)
            creds = flow.run_local_server(port=0)
        with open('token.pickle', 'wb') as token:
            pickle.dump(creds, token)
    return build('photoslibrary', 'v1', credentials=creds, static_discovery=False)

def create_or_get_album(service, title):
    # Note: A smarter butler would search for existing albums first.
    # For simplicity, this creates a new one.
    album_body = {'album': {'title': title}}
    created_album = service.albums().create(body=album_body).execute()
    return created_album['id']

def organize_by_category(service, category_name, target_album_title):
    print(f"Butler is looking for: {category_name}...")
    
    # Google's internal content categories
    # Options: LANDSCAPES, RECEIPTS, CITYSCAPES, DOCUMENTS, WEDDINGS, BIRTHDAYS, PETS, NIGHT, ETC.
    
    request_body = {
        "filters": {
            "contentFilter": {
                "includedContentCategories": [category_name]
            }
        },
        "pageSize": 100
    }

    results = service.mediaItems().search(body=request_body).execute()
    items = results.get('mediaItems', [])

    if not items:
        print("No items found.")
        return

    # Create the album
    album_id = create_or_get_album(service, target_album_title)
    
    # Batch add items (Limit 50 per batch usually)
    item_ids = [item['id'] for item in items]
    
    # The API requires batching
    batch_size = 50
    for i in range(0, len(item_ids), batch_size):
        batch = item_ids[i:i + batch_size]
        body = {'mediaItemIds': batch}
        service.albums().batchAddMediaItems(albumId=album_id, body=body).execute()
        print(f"Moved {len(batch)} photos to album '{target_album_title}'")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    service = get_service()
    
    # --- The Butler's Instructions ---
    # 1. Group all Receipts
    organize_by_category(service, "RECEIPTS", "Start-up Expenses / Receipts")
    
    # 2. Group all Documents
    organize_by_category(service, "DOCUMENTS", "Reference Docs")
    
    # 3. Group Landscapes
    organize_by_category(service, "LANDSCAPES", "Nature Shots")

The "Community" Alternative (No Code)

If the Python script feels too manual, there is a community-built tool that lives in the browser, bypassing the API limits (because it acts as you clicking buttons).

Google Photos Toolkit (GPTK)

  • What it is: A tampermonkey/userscript (JavaScript running in your browser).
  • Why use it: It allows actions the API forbids, like "Select all photos in this album and Move to Trash."
  • Workflow:
    1. Install Tampermonkey extension.
    2. Install the GPTK script.
    3. Open Google Photos. You will see a new toolkit bar.
    4. Run a filter: "Show me all photos < 50KB" (removes blurry junk) or "Show me all duplicates."
    5. Bulk delete.

Summary of Recommendation

Since you have a Mac M2 and an engineering background:

  1. Use the Python Script above to create "Smart Albums" based on Google's AI categories (Receipts, Documents, Pets). This organizes your "view" of the photos without risking data loss.
  2. Use the GPTK (Browser Script) if you need to perform destructive cleanup (Mass Delete/Archive), as the API will not let you do this.
